title: Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack — Exec Readout (H100 / L40S / B200)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack (H100 / L40S / B200)
Executive readout: perf gains, risks, rollout plan, and positioning impact

Presenter: Talia Benson (Eng Program)
Sponsors: Mateo Alvarez (Runtime), Irene Choi (Infra), Neha Kapoor (SRE)
Date: 2025-12-18


Slide 2 — Why this matters (the problem)
• Today, runtime performance depends on “ambient” config drift: defaults + per-pool overrides + ad hoc tuning during incidents.
• We see repeated patterns:
  – Throughput left on the table (conservative defaults)
  – Tail latency regressions when we chase throughput without guardrails
  – OOMs / fragmentation on smaller-memory SKUs under long-context + concurrency
  – Private deployments misconfigured (unknown override precedence, hard to support)
• Customers and prospects increasingly ask for “Redwood-verified performance profiles” with evidence (not just best-effort).


Slide 3 — Project goal (what we’re shipping)
Deliver a versioned, curated “hardware tuning profiles pack” for the serving runtime:
• Per-SKU tuned runtime configs for kernel selection + scheduler + memory/KV-cache behavior
• Safe-by-default presets with explicit workload envelope
• Measurable deltas (tokens/sec, p50/p95, retries, OOM rate)
• Rollout tooling + canary/regression gates + rollback
• Works across Hosted, Dedicated, Private (same schema + loader; controlled override order)

Non-goals (initial release)
• No new kernels from scratch; we tune/route existing implementations
• No bespoke per-customer tuning as part of pack (handled via Solutions/Support)
• No major API changes


Slide 4 — Scope: what is a “profile” (plain English)
A profile is a named config bundle (versioned) that answers:
• Which scheduler/batching behavior to use for common workload shapes
• Which kernel paths/heuristics to prefer by seq-len bucket
• How to allocate KV cache + protect against OOM/fragmentation
• What we will and will not pin (safe knobs only)
• What happens when hardware detection is ambiguous (fallback)

Operationally:
• Runtime selects a profile based on detected GPU SKU (with normalization of vendor strings)
• Operators can override by pool/deployment (Helm/flags) without forking configs
• Runtime logs and metrics surface: selected profile + override source + key knobs


Slide 5 — Hardware targets + maturity
H100 (GA)
• Default-on candidate for Hosted + Dedicated pools
• Most complete validation and stable perf improvements

L40S (GA)
• Default-on candidate for select cost-optimized pools
• Focus: memory guardrails and long-context stability

B200 (EXPERIMENTAL)
• Behind feature flag; opt-in only
• Limited fleet access; version checks required
• Explicit per-region rollback plan (recent canary incident actioned)


Slide 6 — Benchmark methodology (what we measured)
Workload matrix (representative, not exhaustive)
• Model families: chat + instruct (7B–70B), long-context variants where applicable
• Request shapes:
  – Short prompts + longer decodes (chatty)
  – Long prompts + short decodes (RAG / tool routing)
  – Mixed distributions (production-like)
• Streaming + non-streaming
• Concurrency sweep (low → saturation)
• Seq-len buckets (prefill/decode separately)

Metrics
• Throughput: tokens/sec (decode), requests/sec (end-to-end)
• Latency: p50, p95, p99 (prefill, first-token, end-to-end)
• Reliability: OOM rate, retry rate, error rate
• Cost proxy: GPU-seconds per 1M output tokens (normalized)


Slide 7 — H100: top-line results (balanced profile)
H100 “balanced” preset (scheduler + kernel autoselect by seq bucket)
Observed in perf suite + early canary pools:
• +12–18% decode tokens/sec at iso-quality vs baseline runtime defaults
• p50 largely flat (±2%)
• p95 improved for mid-concurrency workloads (3–8%), but sensitive at saturation if fairness knob mis-set
• GPU memory: small increase (KV cache more aggressively utilized) but within guardrails
• Cost proxy: -10–15% GPU-sec / 1M output tokens at common workloads

Notes
• The largest wins come from better kernel path selection in mid-length buckets and more stable continuous batching.
• Tail latency regressions were found during early validation and addressed (see risks/lessons).


Slide 8 — H100: what changed (high-level knobs)
Scheduler
• Continuous batching tuned for better decode efficiency without starving prefill
• Prefill/decode fairness: guardrailed to avoid long prefill blocking first-token latency
• Backpressure: queue limits tuned to reduce p99 blowups under overload

Kernel selection
• Sequence-length bucket heuristics to avoid slow paths for “awkward” middle buckets
• Conservative fallbacks remain in place when detection/telemetry indicates instability

Safety
• Profile includes explicit max queue depth + overflow behavior
• Compatibility logged at startup (runtime version vs profile pack version)


Slide 9 — L40S: top-line results (stability + cost-sensitive throughput)
L40S profile goals: prevent OOM/fragmentation + preserve latency while improving throughput where safe
Observed:
• OOM rate reduced from “non-zero in long-context matrix runs” → near-zero under defined envelope
• p95 stabilized (fewer GC-like stalls due to fragmentation patterns)
• +5–10% tokens/sec in cost-optimized settings when memory pressure is controlled
• Small throughput trade-off in extreme long-context + high concurrency cases (intended, to keep uptime)

Key takeaway
• The L40S profile is primarily a reliability and predictability win; throughput improvements are secondary.


Slide 10 — B200: current status (experimental)
B200 profile is gated due to limited validation time + fleet constraints
What we have
• Experimental profile behind flag with strict software stack version checks
• Early microbench + limited workload matrix runs show strong headroom

Known risk
• One canary pool regression in eu-west triggered a rapid disable; rollback path worked as designed.
• We will not default-enable B200 until:
  – Wider fleet coverage across regions
  – Stable perf-canary thresholds for this SKU
  – Clear driver/CUDA support matrix published for operators


Slide 11 — Positioning impact (why this is a company-level differentiator)
This pack makes “Redwood-verified performance profiles” concrete:
• Faster and cheaper inference is not just “our runtime is fast”; it’s packaged, versioned, and operable.
• Reduces incident volume from mis-tuned settings (esp. Dedicated + Private)
• Enables predictable serving economics across deployments:
  – Hosted: safe defaults by fleet
  – Dedicated: predictable throughput + SLO behavior per pool
  – Private: supportable, auditable config with clear override semantics

Sales/CS narrative
• We can show a repeatable process + benchmark evidence, not one-off tuning.


Slide 12 — Rollout strategy (how we avoid surprises)
Principles
• Stage by pool/region; default-on only after canary gates are green
• Fast, granular rollback (per pool) without redeploying binaries
• Strong observability for “what profile is active” and “what changed”

Phases
1) Internal perf canary (pre-merge + nightly)
2) Hosted canary pools (single region → multi-region)
3) Dedicated pools (selected customers; communicated change window)
4) Private (opt-in via Helm values; documented override order)


Slide 13 — Canary gates (what blocks a rollout)
Perf-canary gates (blocker thresholds; exact values in dashboards)
• Latency regression: p95 first-token and end-to-end must remain within bounds vs baseline
• Throughput: tokens/sec should improve or remain neutral within noise bands
• Reliability: error rate / retry rate must not regress; OOM must remain below threshold
• Stability: sustained runs required (avoid “one lucky run”)

Operational gates
• Profile selection metrics present and correct
• Debug endpoint can dump effective config (including override sources)
• Oncall can disable profile per pool quickly


Slide 14 — Override order + supportability (operator controls)
We standardized precedence to prevent “mystery behavior”:
1) Explicit per-deployment override (e.g., Helm values / runtime flags)
2) Per-pool defaults (fleet config)
3) Hardware profile pack selected by GPU SKU
4) Runtime compiled defaults (lowest priority)

Support playbook improvement
• Runtime logs: selected profile + profile pack version + compatibility matrix
• Metrics: profile_name, override_source, key knob values for dashboards


Slide 15 — Risks and mitigations (what can go wrong)
1) Tail latency regressions (throughput tuning harms p95/p99)
• Mitigation: separate “balanced” vs “throughput-first” modes; default to balanced; canary gates emphasize tail
• Mitigation: fairness guardrails + regression tests around prefill/decode interplay

2) Hardware variance (HBM size, clocks, PCIe vs SXM, MIG)
• Mitigation: guardrails keyed off detected capabilities; conservative fallback when ambiguous
• Mitigation: normalize GPU SKU strings from different providers

3) Config drift / hard-to-reproduce issues
• Mitigation: profile pack versioning + compatibility matrix logged at startup
• Mitigation: CLI to dump effective runtime config; reduce default churn by normalization

4) Perf-canary noise / false positives
• Mitigation: tighten runner reliability; require multi-run confirmation; tune thresholds with SRE input


Slide 16 — Incident learnings (what we fixed during validation)
H100 prefill/decode fairness regression
• Symptom: p95 first-token regression after enabling early preset under certain concurrency ranges
• Root cause: fairness parameters interacted poorly with streaming workloads + long prefill bursts
• Fix: adjust fairness bounds and add regression test; ship guardrails in profile

B200 eu-west canary regression
• Action taken: disable experimental profile for that pool; confirm rollback and alerting paths
• Follow-up: stronger version checks + tighter gating; require broader validation before re-enabling


Slide 17 — “Expected behavior” vs guarantees (messaging alignment)
We will document:
• Expected improvements and known trade-offs per profile
• Workload assumptions (seq-len mix, concurrency ranges, streaming behavior)
• Known failure modes + mitigations (what toggle to flip, what to check)

We will avoid:
• Implying contractual latency guarantees from a profile alone
• Overpromising across unsupported workloads/hardware variants


Slide 18 — Timeline and milestones (current status)
Done / in progress
• Schema + validation + loader (runtime)
• H100 balanced preset validated; throughput-first mode available but not default
• L40S memory/KV budgeting guardrails implemented
• Metrics + dashboards segmentation by selected profile
• Canary gates integrated

Next 2–4 weeks
• Expand workload matrix realism (prompt mix, tool-calling patterns)
• Finalize docs + operator runbook; internal training for oncall + CS
• Default-on staged rollout for H100 + L40S in Hosted (by region)

B200
• Continue opt-in experimentation; widen fleet access; publish support matrix


Slide 19 — Decisions / asks (exec support needed)
1) Approve default-on rollout for H100 balanced profile in Hosted (staged by region) once gates are green.
2) Approve default-on rollout for L40S profile in cost-optimized pools (staged; with OOM/latency gates).
3) Reconfirm B200 remains experimental/opt-in only until exit criteria are met.
4) Resource asks:
• Dedicated perf lab time on B200 (fleet access + stable runners)
• SRE capacity for rollout readiness review and alert routing
• Docs time to finalize operator + customer-facing internal guidance
